newsitem.title: GERMANY: Spain's Rato affirms economic stability commitment.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Rato affirms economic stability commitment.

text.p: Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato on Wednesday affirmed Spain's commitment to economic stability, a day after a top German official hinted only a few countries were ready to be in at the start of the EU single currency.

"Trying to reach real convergence, without any consideration towards stability, would be a short-sighted approach," Rato told the Federation of German Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), according to an advance text of his speech.
"Within months this policy would backfire and lead to economic instability," he said. "The only way to achieve progress in real convergence is through macroeconomic stability."
Rato also reaffirmed Spain's determination to be one of the founding members of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"Let me stress that the participation of Spain in the single currency right from the start is a commitment shared by a great majority of the Spanish political parties and of Spanish citizens," he said.

German Finance Ministry number two Juergen Stark on Tuesday told a conference that although some member states would qualify on paper for EMU at the outset, they should forego the political prestige and instead take time to stabilise their economies.
Stark is known as a hardliner on monetary union and his comments appeared aimed at countries like Italy and Spain that have not yet established a track record of exchange rate stability.

Spain's young conservative government has invested huge political capital in qualifying for EMU, and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar emphatically reaffirmed Spain's intention to be in the EMU starting group in an interview with the weekly Die Zeit.
Aznar and other cabinet ministers were due to join Rato in Bonn on Thursday for an annual round of consultations with Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his cabinet.

Rato listed a number of measures designed to ensure Spain stays within the Maastricht criteria from 1999 onwards, in conformity with the Stability Pact agreed by EU members at their Dublin summit last month.
Among these was a domestic stability pact between the central and regional governments.

Rato said the good results of Spain's stability-oriented policies showed that EMU was "the starting point for a virtuous circle of low inflation, low deficit and higher real growth and employment creation..."
